title: Locality-Controlled Out-of-Distribution Guidance for Robust Regulatory DNA Sequence Design

paper.title: Locality-Controlled Out-of-Distribution Guidance for Robust Regulatory DNA Sequence Design
paper.abstract:
Abstract Designing regulatory DNA sequences for targeted gene-expression control is an important challenge.
Recent approaches frame this task as property-conditioned generation, where diffusion models trained on natural sequences are guided toward high predicted activity through reward-based fine-tuning or sampling-time guidance.
We show that single-reward evaluation can obscure reward-hacking behavior.
By decomposing evaluation into property, novelty, and plausibility, we identify an empirically underexplored region of the evaluation space in which all three objectives are satisfied, but no existing baseline succeeds.
We postulate that this gap arises because prior methods treat guidance primarily as a matter of magnitude.
In regulatory DNA, however, sequence grammar is spatially nonuniform: motif positions are sensitive to perturbation, while background regions allow more exploration.
We therefore propose LocoGen by reformulating guidance as a problem of locality . LocoGen learns an invariant motif mask through sequence-level invariance learning to protect motif positions, while applying OOD damping only to background positions.
It operates at sampling time on a frozen diffusion backbone, without retraining the backbone.
Across HepG2, K562, and SK-N-SH, LocoGen reaches this previously underexplored region of the property–novelty–plausibility space.
Code is available at https://github.com/Lotfollahi-lab/LocoGen .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models are powerful generative models used in many domains, including images, language, molecules, and biological sequences. Beyond unconditional generation, recent work increasingly focuses on property-conditioned generation, such as generating regulatory DNA sequences that optimize a target property (e.g. gene expression). These advances make diffusion models useful for de novo regulatory DNA design, where candidate sequences can be generated and tested in a lab-in-the-loop setting. We argue that the generated candidates must satisfy three axes simultaneously: (i) high target property , (ii) novelty , and (iii) plausibility —preservation of the natural grammar of regulatory DNA (e.g. motif usage diversity/density). No single axis suffices. High property without plausibility fails to reproduce in the wet lab; high novelty without plausibility drifts off the functional manifold; high property without novelty merely reproduces the training distribution. Only when all three axes are jointly satisfied is a candidate worth its wet-lab budget. To date, DNA sequence generative models have largely treated candidate generation as a single-objective problem: maximizing the target property. However, when evaluation is decomposed into property, novelty, and plausibility, methods that appear strong under single-axis evaluation reveal trade-offs on the remaining axes (Fig. 1 B). Moreover, their apparent property gains often arise not from targeted regulatory improvement, but from distortions of regulatory motif structure, exposing a common limitation of existing guidance methods (§ 5.3 ). Although these methods differ in their reward-hacking mechanisms, they all control optimization through a single scalar magnitude knob (e.g. guidance scale) without specifying where in the sequence the reward should act. This is problematic because regulatory DNA grammar is positional: motif sites are highly constrained, whereas intervening background regions are more permissive. Thus, in the property–novelty–plausibility design space, current baselines fall short of the desired regime: high activity on both readouts, high novelty, and low compositional deviation. We call this unoccupied region the empty corner , and ask whether guidance can shift the empirical trade-off landscape toward it. We propose LocoGen , a locality-controlled guidance method for de novo regulatory DNA generation (Fig. 1 A). Rather than increasing guidance globally, LocoGen controls where it acts. A masked separator model identifies foreground and background positions with an invariant mask; during sampling, out-of-distribution (OOD) guidance is applied only to background positions. This generates novel sequences in permissive regions while preserving regulatory motifs, thereby improving novelty without sacrificing enhancer-like composition or functional activity.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: • Diagnostic framework. We introduce a three-axis evaluation framework for regulatory DNA generation: property, novelty, and compositional plausibility. It reveals two reward-hacking modes concealed by single-axis evaluation: predictor-specific motif concentration and global compositional drift in previous DNA sequence generative models. • Locality-controlled guidance. We reformulate sampling-time guidance as a locality problem and instantiate it as localized OOD control with an invariant subsequence mask. The method operates on a frozen backbone, requires no retraining, and exposes per-position spatial control absent from standard classifier-guidance methods. Figure 1 : LocoGen balances property, novelty, and plausibility.

sections.heading: Discrete diffusion and flow matching on biological sequences.
sections.text: Two frameworks have emerged for generative modeling of categorical sequences. Discrete diffusion operates directly on categorical sequences and learns to denoise progressively masked tokens ( Austin et al., 2021 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Lou et al., 2024 ) . Continuous diffusion and flow matching instead work in a continuous relaxation of the categorical space, typically the probability simplex whose vertices correspond to the discrete tokens ( Stark et al., 2024 ; Davis et al., 2024 ) Both have been applied to regulatory DNA design ( Stark et al., 2024 ; DaSilva et al., 2026 ; Tang et al., 2025 ) . We build on the discrete diffusion line, using a pretrained masked discrete diffusion language model (MDLM) ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ) as a backbone and steering generation with inference-time guidance.

sections.heading: Reward-based fine-tuning of diffusion backbones.
sections.text: A first family of methods directly fine-tunes the backbone against a reward signal, often framed as reinforcement learning. DRAKES ( Wang et al., 2025 ) backpropagates a differentiable reward to pre-trained masked discrete diffusion model; DRaFT ( Clark et al., 2024 ) applies the same differentiable-reward principle in the continuous setting. When the reward is non-differentiable, policy-gradient or gradient-free alternatives are used instead ( Cao et al., 2025 ) . These methods can each optimize toward a particular property, but they do not expose a post-hoc control knob: changing the target reward generally requires re-specifying the training objective and running a separate fine-tuning pass, even when recent variants reduce its cost or handle multiple objectives jointly. Although recent methods reduce the cost of retraining ( Cao et al., 2025 ) , they inherently require backbone retraining for each new objective.

sections.heading: Training-free guidance.
sections.text: Classifier guidance instead allows the guidance signal to be adjusted entirely at inference time through an external scoring network ( Uehara et al., 2025 ; Rojas et al., 2026 ) . DNA-Diffusion ( DaSilva et al., 2026 ) , by contrast, conditions on cell-type labels rather than optimizing a reward, and therefore serves as a non-optimizing reference rather than a competing optimizer. Another method that bypasses backbone retraining is by sampling many candidates and selecting the highest-scoring ones. SVDD ( Li et al., 2024 ) performs soft value-based decoding, evaluating generated candidates at each step and resampling proportionally to a learned value.

sections.heading: 3.4 Classifier guidance with OOD control
4 Method
sections.text: We propose Locogen , a localized sequence generation framework that controls both the magnitude and locality of generated sequences. The uniform application of guidance and OOD control in Eq. 4 encodes an implicit assumption: that all sequence positions should be perturbed by the same amount. We argue this assumption is not perfectly suited for regulatory DNA. Functional motifs occupy a small fraction of each sequence and are highly constrained by sequence grammar, while the remaining background is comparatively unconstrained. Pushing motifs off-manifold destroys the very signal that makes a sequence functional, while pushing background off-manifold contributes novelty without sacrificing function.

sections.heading: Problem formulation.
sections.text: We aim to identify subsequences whose contribution to activity is invariant across data subpopulations, i.e., positions whose predictive role does not change from one subpopulation to another. A straightforward approach is to train an activity predictor and use saliency, but such scores reflect what a single trained model happens to rely on, without explicitly accounting for invariance. We instead build this requirement into the learning objective: the selected positions are encouraged to predict activity equally well across subpopulations .

sections.heading: Problem.
sections.text: The MOOD framework (§ 3.4 ) promotes novel, high-scoring samples by combining sample-level OOD drift with property guidance. For regulatory DNA, this global control is too coarse: without distinguishing constrained motifs from permissive background regions, OOD drift can erase regulatory syntax and compromise activity.

sections.heading: Approach.
sections.text: We let damping act only on positions the separator marks as environment. By restricting OOD control to environment positions, we aim to preserve activity-relevant sequence patterns while encouraging exploration in less constrained regions. This is the localization in LocoGen : a structural prior on where OOD pressure may act, instead of one global knob trading off the two objectives.

sections.heading: Dataset.
sections.text: We follow the experimental setup of DRAKES ( Wang et al., 2025 ) to ensure direct comparability under an established benchmark protocol, adopting the same chromosomal train/test split. The benchmark is based on the publicly available large-scale enhancer dataset of Gosai et al. (2024) , consisting of approximately 700k 200-bp human enhancer sequences with expression measurements quantified in three human cell lines: HepG2, K562, and SK-N-SH.

sections.heading: Generation protocol and evaluation.
sections.text: We follow the DRAKES evaluation scheme ( Wang et al., 2025 ) : each method generates N = 640 N{=}640 sequences (20 batches × \times 32), which are then re-scored by independent held-out oracle to avoid circularity between guidance and evaluation. This oracle has three MPRA readouts (HepG2, K562, SK-N-SH), is never used for any method’s guidance or fine-tuning, and serves as our canonical MPRA-property axis. As a second, MPRA-independent functional readout, we additionally report chromatin accessibility from the binary ATAC classifier ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . For more detailed evaluation protocol, see § S2 .

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare LocoGen with baselines spanning three categories of regulatory sequence generative models: (1) non-optimizing references: MDLM ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ) (2) Reward-based fine-tuning: DRAKES ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , and (3) Training-free guidance: MDLM with classifier guidance (MDLM+CG), SVDD ( Li et al., 2024 ) , and DNA-diffusion ( DaSilva et al., 2026 ) . All baselines are run with their authors’ released checkpoints and original decoding hyperparameters. We acknowledge concurrent DNA generative models, e.g GLID2E ( Cao et al., 2025 ) , Ctrl-DNA ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , and GFlowNet ( Bengio et al., 2021 ) , but do not include them as baselines since no public checkpoints are available and retraining their upstream models is out of scope. Computation resource requirements are reported in § S1.5 .

sections.heading: 5.2 Three-axis evaluation framework
sections.text: We evaluate a generated set 𝒳 ∗ = { x ∗ ( i ) } i = 1 N \mathcal{X}^{*}=\{x^{*(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N} against the training set 𝒳 = { x ( j ) } j = 1 M \mathcal{X}=\{x^{(j)}\}_{j=1}^{M} along three axes, (1) property, (2) novelty, and (3) compositional plausibility under a fixed protocol decoupled from each method’s training or guidance loop. All metrics are reported as mean ± \pm standard deviation across three sampling seeds.

sections.heading: 5.2.1 Property axis.
sections.text: We assess functional activity using two complementary held-out predictors from Wang et al. (2025) : regulatory potency, measured by target gene expression, and chromatin accessibility, which is required for transcription factors to bind regulatory sequences and modulate gene expression. See § S2.2 for details.

sections.heading: Pred-activity
sections.text: We use an independently released oracle that maps a sequence to a scalar prediction of gene expression, with separate heads for cell lines c ∈ { HepG2 , K562 , SK ​ - ​ N ​ - ​ SH } c\in\{\mathrm{HepG2},\mathrm{K562},\mathrm{SK\text{-}N\text{-}SH}\} . For each cell line, we report the median predicted activity over generated samples.

sections.heading: ATAC_acc.
sections.text: We use an independently released classifier that maps each sequence to a predicted probability of chromatin accessibility, formulated as a binary classification task distinguishing accessible from inaccessible sequences. We report the mean predicted accessibility over generated samples.

Given hits / seq \mathrm{hits}/\mathrm{seq} of natural sequences, deviation in either direction indicates motif under- or over-insertion.

sections.heading: 5.3 Diagnostic: two structurally distinct hacking modes
sections.text: Among baselines, both SVDD and DRAKES successfully push predicted activity upward, but along distinct non-natural directions. Natural enhancers rely on the combinatorial cooperation of multiple TFs, with motifs distributed at a characteristic density. Beyond previously reported metrics, we assess how closely the functional motif composition of generated sequences approaches that of natural regulatory sequences by measuring motif usage diversity and density via Δ \Delta Gini and Δ \Delta hits. A large Δ \Delta Gini indicates that generated sequences are dominated by a few repeated motifs, while a large Δ \Delta hits indicates stuffed motif within a sequence. In either case, predictor scores can remain high even as the sequence drifts away from natural enhancer composition. Figure 2 : Diagnostics of existing sequence design baselines.

sections.heading: SVDD: motif inflation.
sections.text: In SVDD, motif density per sequence inflates to 1.44 × 1.44\times the natural baseline ( Δ ​ hits = 0.248 \Delta\,\text{hits}=0.248 , from 0.561 0.561 to 0.809 0.809 ; Tab. 1 , Fig. 2 A1), while motif usage concentrates on a narrow subset of the JASPAR repertoire ( Δ ​ Gini = 0.231 \Delta\,\text{Gini}=0.231 , from 0.308 0.308 to 0.539 0.539 ; Tab. 1 ,Fig. 2 A2). Repeated use of functionally important motifs is itself biologically plausible; the pathology of SVDD, rather, is that it repeats a single motif up to saturation within a single sequence. Together, these observations suggest that SVDD raises predicted activity by repeatedly stuffing a small set of presumably activity-driving motifs into sequence, rather than by employing the diverse motif vocabulary characteristic of natural enhancers.

sections.heading: DRAKES: GC-rich composition drift.
sections.text: Unlike SVDD, DRAKES does not overpack motifs ( Δ ​ hits = 0.06 \Delta\,\text{hits}=0.06 ; Tab. 1 , Fig. 2 A1-2), but its motif usage is still skewed toward a narrow subset of the JASPAR repertoire ( Δ ​ Gini = 0.261 \Delta\,\text{Gini}=0.261 ; Tab. 1 ). To understand which motifs DRAKES preferentially favors, we examined the over-represented entries and found that they are predominantly GC-rich (Fig. 2 B1). The composition of the generated sequences depart substantially from the natural compositional baseline (Fig. 2 B2). Together, these observations suggest that DRAKES inflates predicted activity by drifting toward a generic GC-rich background, rather than by concentrating on the functionally relevant motifs of the target cell line.

Tables 1 , S4 , S5 , and Figure 1 show that LocoGen occupies a distinct region of the three-axis benchmark space. Single-axis optimization leads to clear trade-offs: SVDD and DRAKES obtain the strongest property scores but incur large plausibility shifts, whereas DNA-Diff closely matches the training distribution but yields weaker property optimization and limited rarity. sections.heading: (ii)
sections.text: To distinguish the contribution of learned localization from that of generative optimization, we conducted a non-generative control experiment based on a segment-and-shuffle strategy (Tab. S7 ). See details in § S3.3.2 . LearnedMask outperformed heuristic segmentation methods (e.g., predicted activity of 0.442 vs. 0.359 for GC-content masking under uniform shuffling), suggesting that learned localization better identifies activity-relevant regions. Nevertheless, preserving these regions while shuffling the background remained substantially less effective than full LocoGen (predicted activity: 0.442 vs. 4.679; ATAC accessibility: 0.280 vs. 0.716). These results suggest that localization alone is insufficient to reproduce LocoGen’s performance, highlighting the importance of combining learned localization with a property-guided generative model.

sections.heading: 5.5 Robustness to evaluation configuration
sections.text: To verify that the balanced three-axis profile is not an artifact of our evaluation setup, we evaluated LocoGen under (1) independent oracles and (2) a hyperparameter sweep. We first re-evaluated all methods with two publicly available alternative oracles released by prior work ( Li et al., 2024 ; Genentech, 2025 ) . See § S3.4 for details. Swapping in these oracles leaves most of the ranking intact (Tab. S8 , S9 , S10 ). Its three-axis profile is therefore not tied to a specific oracle. Next, we swept LocoGen and every baseline over the ranges given in each method’s paper or official repository; see § S3.5 for details. Across these sweeps, LocoGen retains its balanced three-axis advantage, confirming that the result does not rely on a cherry-picked hyperparameter configuration.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We studied sampling-time guidance for regulatory DNA generation and showed that single-axis evaluation can obscure distinct reward-hacking modes. By decomposing evaluation into property, novelty, and plausibility, we identified a desirable region that existing baselines fail to reach. We showed that this gap can be addressed by treating guidance as a problem of locality (which positions to modify) rather than scalar strength. Implemented as localized OOD control with an invariant motif mask, this approach improves the three-axis balance on a frozen backbone without retraining. More broadly, our results suggest that locality-aware guidance may be useful in other structured domains with spatially or functionally nonuniform grammars. See § S4 for further discussions on limitations and impact of this work.

The predictor reads out the invariant subsequence through a 2-layer head on global mean pooling, y ^ inv = W 2 ​ ReLU ​ ( W 1 ​ 1 L ​ ∑ ℓ = 1 L h ψ ​ ( x inv ) ℓ ) , W 1 ∈ ℝ H × H , W 2 ∈ ℝ 1 × H , \hat{y}^{\text{inv}}\;=\;W_{2}\,\mathrm{ReLU}\!\Bigl(W_{1}\,\tfrac{1}{L}\textstyle\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}h_{\psi}(x^{\text{inv}})_{\ell}\Bigr),\qquad W_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times H},\;W_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times H}, (S4) while the environment encoder produces a single embedding per sequence, g ω ​ ( x env ) = 1 L ​ ∑ ℓ = 1 L g ~ ω ​ ( x env ) ℓ ∈ ℝ H , g_{\omega}(x^{\text{env}})\;=\;\tfrac{1}{L}\textstyle\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\tilde{g}_{\omega}(x^{\text{env}})_{\ell}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{H}, (S5) where g ~ ω \tilde{g}_{\omega} denotes the convolutional trunk before pooling. We write g ω ​ ( x env ) g_{\omega}(x^{\text{env}}) for the pooled embedding throughout, as in § 4.1 . The three networks share architecture but not weights, and only S ϕ S_{\phi} and h ψ h_{\psi} are trained: g ω g_{\omega} is randomly initialized and kept frozen. A trainable environment encoder can lower ℒ inv \mathcal{L}_{\text{inv}} by collapsing the embedding space itself rather than by improving the partition; tying g ω g_{\omega} to h ψ h_{\psi} has the same effect, since the predictor’s collapse attractor ( x inv → b ¯ x^{\text{inv}}\!\to\!\bar{b} , y ^ inv \hat{y}^{\text{inv}} constant) would then corrupt the embedding space used for k k -means (§ S1.3.3 ). Freezing g ω g_{\omega} leaves the separator as the only route by which the environment partition can change, which is what makes the V-REx penalty informative about the mask.

sections.heading: Mask anchoring ( ℒ reg \mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}} ).
sections.text: A symmetric quadratic penalty pulling the average mask density to the target ρ \rho , with an optional bimodal sub-term: ℒ reg = ( M ¯ − ρ ) 2 + λ bim ​ M ⁡ ( 1 − M ) ¯ , M ¯ = 1 B ​ L ​ ∑ n , ℓ M ℓ ( n ) . \mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}}\;=\;(\bar{M}-\rho)^{2}\;+\;\lambda_{\text{bim}}\,\overline{M(1-M)},\qquad\bar{M}\;=\;\tfrac{1}{BL}\textstyle\sum_{n,\ell}M^{(n)}_{\ell}. (S6) The first term is expected- L 0 L_{0} anchoring [ Louizos et al., 2017 ] . We set λ bim = 0 \lambda_{\text{bim}}\!=\!0 : with λ bim > 0 \lambda_{\text{bim}}\!>\!0 the { 0 , 1 } \{0,1\} valleys become attractors and combine with the mean term to collapse the separator within the first epoch. The target density ρ \rho is held as a frozen buffer rather than a trainable parameter; when made learnable it gets pulled toward M ¯ \bar{M} , which hollows out the penalty whenever the mask collapses.

sections.heading: Spatial smoothness ( ℒ smooth \mathcal{L}_{\text{smooth}} ).
sections.text: A fused-lasso total-variation penalty on adjacent mask values [ Javanmardi et al., 2016 ] : ℒ smooth = 1 B ⁡ ( L − 1 ) ​ ∑ n ∑ ℓ = 1 L − 1 | M ℓ + 1 ( n ) − M ℓ ( n ) | . \mathcal{L}_{\text{smooth}}\;=\;\tfrac{1}{B(L-1)}\textstyle\sum_{n}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L-1}\bigl|M^{(n)}_{\ell+1}-M^{(n)}_{\ell}\bigr|. (S7) This encourages contiguous selected blocks rather than scattered single positions, consistent with the cis-regulatory grammar in which functional elements occupy short contiguous motifs.

sections.heading: V-REx variance estimator.
sections.text: ℒ inv \mathcal{L}_{\text{inv}} in Eq. 7 is computed in its biased form. Environments containing fewer than two samples are dropped from the variance estimate; if fewer than two environments survive, we set ℒ inv = 0 \mathcal{L}_{\text{inv}}\!=\!0 for that batch.

sections.heading: S1.3.3 Environment inference by k k -means
sections.text: Because x env x^{\text{env}} is defined by the current mask, the inferred environments shift as S ϕ S_{\phi} is updated. We therefore refit k k -means at the start of every epoch, so that the V-REx penalty is always measured against the partition induced by the current mask, and hold the labels fixed within the epoch, which prevents the separator from lowering Var e ​ [ R e ] \mathrm{Var}_{e}[R_{e}] by reshuffling the environments themselves (the standard GIL alternating optimization [ Li et al., 2022 ] ). Writing j j for the epoch index, one round proceeds as follows.

sections.heading: Step 1 — Snapshot collection.
sections.text: At the start of each epoch j ≥ t warmup j\geq t_{\text{warmup}} , a copy Θ j \Theta_{j} of the current parameters is frozen; since g ω g_{\omega} is already frozen, the snapshot pins the separator, and hence the mask that defines x env x^{\text{env}} . Up to N km = 8192 N_{\text{km}}\!=\!8192 samples are drawn from the train loader and their environment embeddings g ω ​ ( x env , Θ j ) g_{\omega}(x^{\text{env}};\Theta_{j}) are collected. For this pass alone we use hard-input mixing: the fill token b b is not injected, so k k -means clusters on actual background nucleotide content rather than on a b b -contaminated mixture.

sections.heading: Step 2 — k k -means fit.
sections.text: Lloyd’s algorithm [ Lloyd, 1982 ] is run with E = 3 E\!=\!3 clusters and T km = 20 T_{\text{km}}\!=\!20 iterations, initialized by random-sample seeding indexed by the epoch number. The resulting centroids { c e } e = 1 E ⊂ ℝ H \{c_{e}\}_{e=1}^{E}\subset\mathbb{R}^{H} are cached.

sections.heading: Step 3 — Minibatch assignment.
sections.text: During each training step within the epoch, samples are assigned to the nearest cached centroid under squared ℓ 2 \ell_{2} distance: e ^ ( n ) = arg ⁡ min e ∈ { 1 , … , E } ⁡ ‖ g ω ​ ( x env ​ ( n ) , Θ j ) − c e ‖ 2 2 . \hat{e}^{(n)}\;=\;\arg\min_{e\in\{1,\dots,E\}}\bigl\|g_{\omega}(x^{\text{env}(n)};\Theta_{j})-c_{e}\bigr\|_{2}^{2}. (S8) These labels feed ℒ inv \mathcal{L}_{\text{inv}} (Eq. 7 ). Because both the centroids and the embeddings are taken from the same frozen snapshot Θ j \Theta_{j} , environment labels and centroids stay mutually consistent for the whole epoch.

sections.heading: Warmup.
sections.text: For the first t warmup = 1 t_{\text{warmup}}\!=\!1 epoch no centroids exist; we set ℒ inv = 0 \mathcal{L}_{\text{inv}}\!=\!0 and train as pure ERM on x inv x^{\text{inv}} . Subsequently the refit runs at the start of every epoch.

sections.heading: S1.4 Localization-guided sampler
sections.text: The sampler operates entirely at inference time on frozen components: the MDLM prior p θ p_{\theta} , the separator S ϕ S_{\phi} , and the activity guidance model r ξ r_{\xi} . At each reverse step t → s t\!\to\!s it evaluates p θ p_{\theta} once, forms the x 0 x_{0} -prediction x ^ 0 \hat{x}_{0} , queries the separator to obtain M t = S ϕ ​ ( x ^ 0 ) M_{t}=S_{\phi}(\hat{x}_{0}) , and combines the three factors of Eq. 8 : the localized damping d ℓ , t ​ ( γ ) d_{\ell,t}(\gamma) of Eq. 9 , the MDLM unmasking mass Δ t → s \Delta_{t\to s} , and the auto-balanced property pull η t ∇ r \eta_{t}\nabla r of Eq. 10 . Damping is gated by two thresholds: it acts only where M t , ℓ < τ M M_{t,\ell}<\tau_{M} , i.e. on environment positions, and only for t < τ time t<\tau_{\text{time}} , i.e. in the second half of sampling, where x ^ 0 \hat{x}_{0} is informative enough for S ϕ S_{\phi} to classify positions reliably. Because already-decoded positions are frozen by the point mass of § S1.2.2 , damping is in effect restricted to still-masked positions.

sections.heading: Sentinel-aware normalization.
sections.text: The auto-balance of Eq. 10 normalizes the property pull by the mean magnitude of the prior log-probabilities. DRAKES [ Wang et al., 2025 ] writes a large negative sentinel at positions whose token has already been determined, in order to block re-sampling. Taken without filtering, these sentinel entries dominate | log ⁡ p θ | ¯ \overline{|\log p_{\theta}|} , inflate the ratio, and pin η t \eta_{t} at its cap η max \eta_{\max} at every step, which silently disables auto-balance. We therefore restrict the mean to non-sentinel entries ( log ⁡ p θ > − 10 5 \log p_{\theta}>-10^{5} ). The same correction is applied when running the classifier-guided baselines, so that no method is penalized by this implementation detail.

sections.heading: Finalization.
sections.text: Tokens are drawn from the renormalized categorical distribution over the four nucleotide channels, with the copy rule of MDLM keeping already unmasked positions fixed. After the final reverse step, one additional forward pass with per-position arg ⁡ max \arg\max removes any residual mask tokens, as in DRAKES [ Wang et al., 2025 ] . sections.heading: S1.5 Computational cost
sections.text: All experiments were run on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU per job, with 16 CPU cores and 40 GB of host RAM. Training the masked separator required approximately 5.5 hours per epoch, with peak host-side RAM usage of 4.6 GB. For sequence generation, sampling 640 sequences with 128 reverse-diffusion steps took 191 wall-clock seconds per random seed, with peak host-side RAM usage of 3.5 GB.

sections.heading: Δ \Delta Gini.
sections.text: We scan generated/training sequences against the JASPAR motif database TF position-specific scoring matrices [ Rauluseviciute et al., 2024 ] , thresholded at false positive rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} under a uniform ACGT background. Following Gosai et al. [2024] , motifs are restricted to those whose constituent TF subunits are all expressed at TPM > 1 \mathrm{TPM}>1 in the target cell type. The Gini coefficient over per-motif counts f = ( f 1 , … , f R ) f=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{R}) sorted by ascending order is G ⁡ ( f ) = 1 R ​ ( R + 1 − 2 ​ ∑ r ( R + 1 − r ) ​ f ( r ) ∑ r f ( r ) ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] . G(f)=\tfrac{1}{R}\!\left(R+1-2\,\tfrac{\sum_{r}(R+1-r)\,f_{(r)}}{\sum_{r}f_{(r)}}\right)\in[0,1].

sections.heading: S2.2 Baseline re-scoring and the DRAKES oracle
sections.text: To avoid circularity from using the same predictor for both classifier-guided generation and evaluation, we used separate independent oracles for generation guidance and sequence evaluation, following the DRAKES protocol [ Wang et al., 2025 ] . Specifically, reward_oracle_ft.ckpt is used only for guidance or reward-based fine-tuning, whereas evaluation is performed using the separately distributed reward_oracle_eval.ckpt . This held-out evaluator is a gReLU EnformerPretrainedModel with three MPRA readouts corresponding to HepG2, K562, and SK-N-SH, and never contributes to the guidance or fine-tuning signal of any method. As a second functional readout independent of MPRA, we additionally report chromatin accessibility from the binary ATAC classifier binary_atac_cell_lines.ckpt [ Wang et al., 2025 ] ; the two predictors are trained independently.

sections.heading: S3.2 Masked separator faithfully disentangles invariant and environmental subsequences.
sections.text: We next asked whether the masked separator module recovers a meaningful invariant/environmental decomposition. Three lines of evidence support that it does (Fig. S1 ). First, the three environmental subsequences exhibit clearly distinct GC-content distributions while the invariant subsequence sits near the natural baseline (Fig. S1 A), and the same separation holds in 3-mer PCA space, where each environment forms a distinct cluster around its own centroid (Fig. S1 B). Second, the invariant subsequence is enriched for canonical activity-driving JASPAR motifs, predominantly ETS-family factors (Fig. S1 C). Third, ablating only the invariant subsequence causes a substantially larger drop in oracle-predicted activity than ablating an equally-sized random region (Fig. S1 D), showing that the invariant region is functionally responsible for the predicted activity rather than being an arbitrary partition. Figure S1 : Sequence-level invariance learning recovers regulatory grammar.

sections.text: To better interpret the global-OOD setting in § 5.4.1 , we conducted an additional experiment in which the same number of masked positions was distributed uniformly at random across the sequence (Fig. S2 ). We confirmed that these randomly selected positions exhibited minimal overlap with the invariant region. Figure S2 : The learnt invariant region is not a random subset of positions. (A) For ten HepG2 enhancers, the learnt invariant mask (dark) and a count-matched random mask (purple) along the 200bp window; the light band is the OOD-damped background. Both masks select the same number of positions, so any difference in the ablation is attributable to which positions are spared rather than how many. sections.heading: S3.3.1 Effect of OOD control strength
sections.text: Table S6 studies the effect of the OOD control strength γ \gamma . Without OOD control the model achieves reasonable predicted activity but shows weak ATAC accessibility, low authenticity, limited rarity, and a large deviation in | Δ ​ Gini | |\Delta\text{Gini}| . Increasing γ \gamma to 0.3 substantially improves ATAC accessibility, authenticity, rarity, and both plausibility metrics, indicating that moderate OOD control leads to generate more plausible sequences. At γ = 0.7 \gamma=0.7 , LocoGen achieves the best authenticity, rarity, and | Δ ​ Gini | |\Delta\text{Gini}| , while also maintaining strong predicted activity and the highest ATAC accessibility. Although γ = 0.3 \gamma=0.3 gives slightly higher pred-activity and the lowest | Δ ​ hits | |\Delta\text{hits}| , the γ = 0.7 \gamma=0.7 setting provides the most balanced operating point across property, novelty, and plausibility. These results support the role of OOD control as a calibration mechanism that controls the trade-off between aggressive property optimization and distributional realism. sections.heading: S3.5 Robust to hyperparameter sweep
sections.text: We ran a hyperparameter sweep of both our method and the baselines, sweeping each over the range specified in its paper or official repository. sections.heading: S4.1 Limitations.
sections.text: Our experiments are conducted on a single backbone, MDLM, to isolate the effect of localized OOD guidance from backbone-dependent variation. Validation on alternative backbones, such as flow matching or autoregressive models, and a full comparison across backbones are left to future work. Computational evaluation alone, while standard in this domain, cannot substitute for in vivo experimental validation of generated sequences, a precondition for treating any sampling-time guidance method as practically useful.

sections.heading: S4.2 Social Impact
sections.text: Our work may contribute to bioengineering by improving the ability to generate novel biological sequences beyond the training distribution. Such capability can expand the searchable design space and accelerate the discovery of sequences with useful properties. In practical settings, this could reduce the cost and time required for experimental screening, while supporting applications in therapeutic development, enzyme engineering, antibody design, and synthetic biology. However, the broader impact of biological sequence generation depends on how the technology is used. Since generative models can produce sequences that differ substantially from naturally observed examples, they may also introduce biosafety and dual-use risks. For example, the same methods that help design beneficial proteins or regulatory elements could potentially be misused to explore harmful biological functions. Therefore, responsible use requires careful consideration of dataset provenance, model access, downstream experimental validation, and risk assessment tailored to the intended application.
